query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The onset and progression of the phase transition in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by heterogeneous melting that initiates at surface defect sites. These defects lower the local melting point through enhanced atomic diffusion and configurational entropy, causing localized melting that gradually propagates from the surface inward.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, single-phase FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution and some inherent surface defects.
generation.intervention: A controlled comparison between as-synthesized nanoparticles (with native, defect‐rich surfaces) and nanoparticles whose surfaces have been chemically passivated to reduce defect density.
generation.conditions: Thermal annealing in an inert atmosphere (e.g., high vacuum or argon) with a controlled temperature ramp across the premelting and melting temperature range, including isothermal holds to observe steady-state phase evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface defects and disorder which locally reduce cohesive strength and trigger enhanced atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Defect sites on the nanoparticle surfaces allow increased atomic mobility, which, in the high-entropy context, leads to an earlier local increase in configurational entropy that overcomes local bonding. This initiates a heterogeneous melting front that propagates inward as temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with defect-rich surfaces will begin melting at a lower temperature and display a gradual phase transition from surface to core, while passivated (smoother) surfaces will delay melting onset relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles displaying a uniformly solid-phase structure under lower temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Tested under inert atmosphere conditions to prevent oxidation, with nanoparticle sizes at the scale where surface effects dominate (typically in the single-digit to tens of nanometers), and under controlled heating rates to minimize bulk diffusion effects.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall mechanism is anticipated, the exact quantitative shift in melting onset temperature and the relative influence of atomic diffusion versus the configurational entropy effect remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one retaining their native, defect-rich surfaces and the other modified via a chemical passivation treatment to reduce surface defects. Heat both sets under identical inert atmosphere conditions with a controlled ramp through the premelting regime. Monitor the evolution of the phase changes in real time using in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD).
measurements: Onset temperature of the phase transition (e.g., disappearance or change of solid-phase diffraction peaks)
Progression rate of phase transition (evaluated by liquid fraction or structural markers as a function of temperature/time)
Surface morphology changes tracked via TEM imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated nanoparticles, with reduced surface defects, exhibit the same melting onset and transition progression (in timing and pattern) as the native defect-rich nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that surface-initiated heterogeneous melting governs the phase transition is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).
